definition: Diaphanous means so light and thin as to be almost transparent.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word diaphanous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know diaphanous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A diaphanous scarf of cloud slid across the moon without dimming it.
Sheer stops short of diaphanous — sheer curtains thin the light, while diaphanous fabric seems hardly to be there at all.
Gossamer goes further than diaphanous — gossamer is spider-silk lightness, cloth you could pull through a ring.

Gauzy compares a material to gauze — loosely woven, light, slightly hazy to look through — and it stays a homely, fabric-shop word. Diaphanous is the literary cousin: material so fine it seems almost not to be there, with a shimmer of glamour gauzy never claims.

Translucent states an optical fact: light passes through, but detail blurs — wax paper over a jar, a paper lampshade. The word says nothing about weight or delicacy. Diaphanous describes the material itself: fabric or mist so light and fine it barely interrupts the light crossing it.

Diaphanous goes beyond 'thin' or 'see-through': it names material so light and delicate that it barely interrupts light at all—mist and veils—where 'sheer' still suggests ordinary fabric.
Diaphanous is a literary word for fabrics, wings, mist — anything so fine it barely interrupts the light.
In plain speech, 'sheer' or 'see-through' does the job; reach for diaphanous when you want the shimmer of the thing on the page.
